title: Programming rest days
summary: NH frames rest days as a planned part of the program rather than a break: place them after the hardest lower body days, know they need not be exactly 24 hours, that training seven days a week is possible by manipulating volume, intensity and session timing, and that too many rest days create a 'tonnage ceiling'.
claims: A rest day is programmed and as important as a training day; skipping a session impromptu is a skip day, not a rest day
If you need a rest day because you are burnt out, the programming is wrong; rest should restore just enough to keep performance, progression and tonnage stable
My rest day is fixed on Sunday while my eight-day program rotates around it, so I must control which day precedes it
The days before a rest day should be lower body days: more load, tonnage, fatigue, cardio demand and tendon stress from squats and deadlifts
Do not place a rest day after only one training day without good reason
A rest day need not be 24 hours; with morning and evening sessions it can be half a day or a day and a half
Training seven days a week is possible; reducing volume and intensity, shortening sessions or spacing sessions replicates the effect of a rest day
A typical rest day actually gives about 48 hours between sessions
Let progression, recovery, tendon feel and psychology guide how many rest days you need
More rest days reduce your ability to spread volume and intensity, creating a tonnage ceiling, like capping sessions at one hour
Four rest days a week starts to be too much, though packing matters: three on, four off is worse than alternating days
Natural bodybuilding is a repeated cycle of breaking down and repairing muscle as often as possible
